reasons: Google and Apple sign-in send a fixed placeholder token, so they cannot work for real users.
Mobile registration password rules are weaker than the web rules.
Only the first 243 lines were reviewed, so the remaining layout and styles were not checked.

terms.meaning: One-time password, a short code sent to a phone or email to confirm identity.
A standard way to sign in with another account, such as Google or Apple.
Signing in with a fingerprint or face scan stored on the device.
A fake value used during development in place of a real login key.
The shared place in the mobile app that holds the signed-in session.

sections.name: File setup, AuthTab, AuthMethod
sections.title: Imports and form types
sections.what: Brings in icons, gradients, navigation, the React base, and the shared components, theme, and auth store. Also defines the two sign-in tabs and the two contact methods.
sections.why: These tools and types are needed by the whole screen.
sections.watch_out: The auth store path here is different from the web store file, so the two apps keep separate session code.

sections.name: LoginScreen (part 1)
sections.title: Screen state and action handlers
sections.what: Keeps the typed values, the current step, and the loading state. Handles email sign in or create account, sending a one-time code, and verifying the code. Each shows an alert on failure and moves to the home screen on success.
sections.why: Lets one screen support several sign-in methods while keeping the loading state accurate.
sections.watch_out: The screen moves to the home screen directly after success, so the auth store must save the session before the move.

sections.name: LoginScreen (part 2)
sections.title: Social, fingerprint and reset handlers
sections.what: Handles Google and Apple sign in with a fixed placeholder token, biometric sign in, and password reset. Shows alerts for each outcome.
sections.why: Gives the other sign-in options the same error and loading behavior. The placeholder is a development stand-in noted in a comment.
sections.watch_out: The placeholder token means social sign-in will fail for real users until it is replaced with a real provider token.

sections.name: LoginScreen (part 3)
sections.title: Screen header and form steps
sections.what: Shows the brand area, then the card with three possible views: reset password, one-time code entry, or the main sign-in form.
sections.why: Keeps the sign-in steps on one screen so users keep their place.
sections.watch_out: The one-time code text always shows +91, so users in other countries will see the wrong prefix.

sections.name: LoginScreen (part 4)
sections.title: Sign-in tabs and email or phone forms
sections.what: Shows sign in and create account tabs, email or phone switch, and the matching form. Email form has name for sign up, email, password with show toggle, and forgot password link. Phone form has a fixed +91 prefix and a ten digit number box. Buttons are disabled until the inputs look valid.
sections.why: Lets users pick how to sign in and blocks obviously incomplete submissions before they reach the server.
sections.watch_out: The button check on mobile only requires eight characters for a new account, so passwords accepted here may be rejected by the server or be weaker than the web rules.

sections.name: LoginScreen (part 5)
sections.title: Biometric sign-in and terms text
sections.what: Shows a fingerprint sign-in button only when a biometric session is available. Below the form, a short line links to the Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.
sections.why: Likely reason: offers quick sign-in on phones that support it. The terms line is a standard part of sign-in screens. Reason for the exact placement not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The terms links are styled like links but have no press action in this section, so tapping them does nothing here.

sections.name: LoginScreen (part 6)
sections.title: Remaining style rules for login screen
sections.what: Defines the look of the one-time code boxes, the hidden text field that captures typing, and the terms text. It only sets appearance.
sections.why: Likely reason: the hidden, invisible text field is a common way to take keyboard input while showing separate code boxes. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The hidden input must keep receiving focus for typing to reach the code boxes. Moving or restyling it may break code entry.

summary: The mobile sign-in and create-account screen. It supports email and password, phone with a one-time code, Google and Apple sign-in, fingerprint or face sign-in, and password reset.
purpose: Lets a new or returning user get into the app. It is the main entry point for signed-out users on mobile.
why: Most sign-in choices are on one screen so users do not have to move between pages. Reason for the mock social sign-in is stated in a comment: the real flow is not yet built.
how: The screen keeps the typed values and the current step, which can be sign in, one-time code, or forgot password. Each action calls the auth store, shows an alert on failure, and moves to the home screen on success. The layout switches between email and phone forms, and shows the social buttons below.
inputs: Typed name, email, password, phone number, and one-time code. Taps on tabs, buttons, and social or biometric options.
outputs: A signed-in session through the auth store, navigation to the home screen, or an alert describing the error.
risks: Google and Apple sign-in send a fixed placeholder token, so those buttons will not work in real use. The phone one-time code screen always shows a +91 prefix. The register button checks only password length on mobile, while the web form requires mixed characters. Only the first 243 lines of this file were reviewed in this packet.
debug: If sign-in fails, check the alert text and the matching auth store action. If a button is disabled, check the length and format rules on the form. If social sign-in fails, confirm the placeholder token was replaced with a real one.
